title: Fourteen thousand against one
hookLine: Khara's army against Rama alone; why Hindus call Rama an avatar of Vishnu
carry: avatar: god comes down when dharma falls

cards: Shurpanakha reaches her brother Khara, who rules a garrison of rakshasas in the forest. She falls at his feet, bleeding, and tells him what happened. He sends fourteen warriors to kill the two brothers.
Rama brings them all down. So she goes back to Khara, screaming at him for his weakness. This time Khara marches out himself, with his generals and an army.
The text gives the number: fourteen thousand. The ground shakes. Dust covers the sun.
Against them, in a clearing by a leaf hut: one man with a bow.

teach.b: Rama sees bad omens and makes his plan. He tells Lakshmana: take Sita to a cave in the hills, guard her, and don't come out. Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and walks out alone.
In Valmiki the sages and heavenly beings gather in the sky to watch, afraid for him. The battle is enormous: arrows, chariots, a storm of weapons. And the text keeps coming back to one thing.

teach.h: HE STANDS WHERE HE IS AND WORKS.
teach.b: He stands where he is and works. The army falls, then the generals one by one, then Khara himself. When it's over, Sita comes out of the cave and embraces him.
Epics tell battles big; you don't have to picture it as a news report. But the tradition has a reason for expecting the impossible from Rama. Hindus honor him as an avatar of Vishnu.
Avatar means a coming down. Vishnu is the god who keeps the world going, and when goodness collapses, he comes down to set it right: as a fish, a boar, a man-lion, and here, as a prince with a bow.

On the battlefield you heard on day twenty-one, Krishna makes the promise: whenever dharma falls, I come. That's why many Hindus don't just admire Rama; they pray to him, and simply saying his name, Ram, is a prayer.

teach.h: AVATAR: GOD COMES DOWN WHEN DHARMA FALLS.
teach.b: It's God living a human life: losing his home, keeping his word, standing alone. One more detail. One rakshasa escapes and runs all the way to Lanka.
Tomorrow, the news reaches the king.

how: Hindus honor Rama as an avatar of Vishnu, often shown with blue or dark skin; many repeat his name, Ram, as a prayer, and read his battles as God coming down to restore dharma.

games.q: a friend asks: if Rama is God, why does he lose his home, grieve, and fight at all?
o: for many Hindus, that is what an avatar is: God comes down and lives a real human life to set dharma right.
he's only pretending; nothing can touch him.
Hindus don't think Rama is God at all.
games.why: Hindus honor Rama as Vishnu come down. he loses, grieves and fights as a man, and that is why people pray to him.

practice: Many Hindus say Rama's name when life feels like fourteen thousand against one. If you pray, sit steady and repeat 'Ram' quietly with each breath for two minutes.
If you don't, think of everything coming at you right now and let it feel like fourteen thousand; sit steady, pick the smallest next thing, and hold only that.

wordCard.voice: Khara's army. Fourteen thousand against one; Rama, Vishnu come down, stands steady and wins, and one survivor runs to Lanka.

orig.note: Sanskrit: harsh, sharp; the name of Shurpanakha's brother.

carryVoice: Your line: avatar, God comes down when dharma falls. Fourteen thousand against him, and he stood. That's forty-seven days.
